conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during your stay. You came in today because of shortness of breath, is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. It’s been getting worse over the past few days. I can’t even walk across the room without stopping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned swelling in your legs too, up to your hips?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been building up. I think I’ve gained weight, but I’m not sure how much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You also had some cough with thick, milky sputum, and a fluttery feeling in your chest?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the fluttering comes and goes. And I’ve been more nauseous, not urinating as much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. We’ve checked your labs and chest X-ray. Good news — your heart enzymes are normal, and there’s no pneumonia or fluid in the lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s a relief. But why am I so short of breath then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing issues are most likely due to an asthma flare-up. We heard a lot of wheezing. We’ve started you on albuterol and ipratropium nebulizers to open your airways.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve had asthma for years. But why the swelling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The swelling is likely due to your lipodermatosclerosis — a chronic skin and tissue condition in your legs. We gave you a dose of Lasix to help reduce it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that for a while. But it’s worse now. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s uncomfortable, but not dangerous right now. We’re watching it. We also checked for blood clots with an ultrasound — no clots were found, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, thank you. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. We’re adding a steroid — prednisone — to help calm the inflammation from your asthma flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that the same as the inhaler I use?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, this is a stronger, oral version. It works throughout your body. You’ll take it for a few days, then taper off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve had steroids before. They make me jittery sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. Let us know if it bothers you. We also started an antibiotic — levofloxacin — for possible bronchitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to some antibiotics. Is this one safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your allergies — you’re not allergic to levofloxacin. But we did stop the IV version because of some swelling at the site. Now you’re on the pill form.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I noticed that. So I should keep taking the pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for five days total. But you’ll need to pause your minocycline until you finish the levofloxacin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why is that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re both antibiotics, and we don’t want to overload your system or cause side effects. You can restart minocycline after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. I’m not as short of breath, and the swelling is going down a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your exam shows less wheezing, and your edema is now only down to your knees. You’re responding well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I was worried it was my heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked that too. Your EKG and BNP level suggest no heart failure. The murmur we heard is known — mild aortic stenosis — and hasn’t changed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my vision? I’ve been seeing floaters and flashes in my left eye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I remember. You’re already scheduled to see ophthalmology. Those symptoms could be retinal, so it’s important to get it checked soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve been anxious about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. Your breathing has improved, and your swelling is much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll finish the prednisone taper — 40 mg for two days, then down gradually. And take the levofloxacin for three more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And minocycline?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Restart it after the levofloxacin. Also, we’re sending you home on Lasix 20 mg twice a week to help with the leg swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All the same — Creon for your pancreas, iron, B12, Mirapex, inhalers. Keep using them as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well. We’re clearing you to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Any warning signs I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. If your breathing worsens, or you develop fever, chest pain, or leg swelling that returns quickly, call your clinic or come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the vision issue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep your ophthalmology appointment. If you see a curtain or sudden loss of vision, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll send all your discharge instructions and meds with you. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. Any new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, still feeling better. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Remember your follow-ups — primary care in a week, and eye doctor soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve got them written down. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy, keep up with your inhalers, and don’t stop any meds unless we say so.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care and feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope so. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here if you need us. See you at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll call if anything comes up.
